q_0158.rationale: Follow-up of children treated from birth or within the first 2 months "found long-term complications, such as ovarian dysfunction, cataracts, abnormal speech, cognitive impairment, growth restriction, and motor delay," and "These findings have revealed that eliminating sources of galactose does not significantly improve the outcome" (p. 66).
q_0158.trap: (A) imports the PKU result, where "early childhood treatment with a reduced phenylalanine diet is highly successful at removing the possibility of cognitive impairment." The chapter places these two disorders together precisely so the contrast is visible: diet largely works for PKU and does not fully work for galactosemia.

q_0159.stem: A child with galactosemia is prescribed an oral antibiotic. What is the nurse's specific responsibility?
options: No special precaution is needed for medications

Instruct the parents to ask their pharmacist about the galactose content of any over-the-counter or prescription medication, because lactose is used as a filler and is an unlabeled ingredient in many pharmaceuticals
Substitute an intravenous route for all medications
Give the antibiotic only with soy formula
q_0159.rationale: "Many drugs, such as some of the penicillin preparations, contain lactose as filler and also must be avoided. Unfortunately, lactose is an unlabeled ingredient in many pharmaceuticals," so the instruction is to "ask their local pharmacist about galactose content of any over-the-counter or prescription medication" (p. 66).
q_0159.trap: (A) is the default assumption once the family has learned to read food labels, and it misses the hidden exposure. This is the one instruction unique to galactosemia — reading food labels is not sufficient, because the drug label may not carry the ingredient at all.

q_0160.stem: A nurse explains the difference between genetic screening and genetic diagnostic testing. What distinguishes them?
options: Screening uses blood and diagnostic testing uses tissue
In general, genetic screening targets populations, whereas genetic diagnostic testing targets individuals — and a positive screen is not a diagnosis
Screening is performed prenatally and diagnostic testing after birth
Screening is voluntary and diagnostic testing is mandatory
q_0160.rationale: "In general, genetic screening targets populations, whereas genetic diagnostic testing targets individuals" (p. 68). Screen-positive infants are "immediately referred to a medical center," and "After a positive screen, diagnostic testing must be performed promptly" (pp. 63, 69).
q_0160.trap: (D) inverts a real principle. Voluntary participation is named as one of the first corollaries of any genetic screening program, along with equal access to all, confidentiality, and education and counseling as an integral part.

q_0161.stem: A family is considering genetic testing and asks what screening is for. Which are among the three stated purposes of genetic screening? (Select all that apply.)
options: Early recognition of a disease before signs and symptoms occur, for which effective intervention and therapy exist
Identifying carriers of a genetic disease to maximize parenthood planning options
Obtaining population data on frequency, spectrum, and natural history of genetic variations not currently known to be associated with disease
Determining which family members should be excluded from insurance coverage
q_0161.rationale: These are the three purposes as printed (p. 69), and this list is the chapter's own NCLEX question 3. Screening can occur at four times: preconception screening of selected populations for carriers, screening of relatives of known carriers or affected individuals, postconceptional prenatal screening, and newborn screening.
q_0161.trap: (D) is the one to reject. Purposes 1 and 2 benefit the individual and purpose 3 benefits knowledge — none of the three is about restricting access, and the chapter names confidentiality as a precondition of any screening program.

q_0162.stem: Parents of a healthy 6-year-old whose grandmother has a BRCA mutation ask for their daughter to be tested now. What should the nurse explain?
options: Predisposition testing for adult-onset cancer is discouraged in at-risk children, and carrier testing for children is generally not recommended because the information is for reproductive purposes
Testing should be done immediately so screening can begin
Predisposition genetic testing in children is never performed under any circumstances
The child should be tested but not told the result
q_0162.rationale: "Carrier testing for children is generally not recommended because the information is for reproductive purposes" (p. 69), and predisposition testing for adult-onset cancer "is discouraged in at-risk children" (p. 67).
q_0162.trap: (C) overcorrects into an absolute the chapter does not make. APC testing is done in at-risk children, because a positive result changes their screening now rather than in adulthood. The rule turns on whether the result changes management during childhood — which is also the distinction between presymptomatic testing, at near-100% penetrance, and susceptibility testing, at partial penetrance.

q_0163.stem: A couple asks the genetic counselor what they should do about a future pregnancy given their 25% recurrence risk. How does the chapter describe the counselor's role?
options: Counselors recommend the option with the lowest risk of an affected child
Counselors "do not attempt to make recommendations or decisions for patients when discussing reproductive risks," although they do recommend screening for treatable conditions
Counselors defer entirely to the referring physician
Counselors provide numbers only and do not discuss options
q_0163.rationale: Genetic counselors "do not attempt to make recommendations or decisions for patients when discussing reproductive risks," though they do recommend screening for treatable conditions (p. 72). The nurse also teaches that each pregnancy is an independent event.
q_0163.trap: (A) is the expectation families arrive with, and it is what makes the non-directive stance worth stating out loud. Note the boundary: non-directiveness applies to reproductive decisions, not to recommending screening for a condition that can be treated.

q_0164.stem: Which assessment findings should alert the nurse to a possible need for further genetic evaluation? (Select all that apply.)
options: Limb abnormalities, asymmetry, and hyperextensible joints
Recurrent ear infection, pneumonia, and poor healing of the umbilicus
Developmental and speech delays or loss of developmental milestones
Recurrent digestive difficulties
Recurrent urinary tract problems
q_0164.rationale: These are three of Box 3.7's eleven categories — skeletal abnormalities, recurrent infection or immunodeficiency, and development and speech delays (p. 72). This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 5. The footnote is the rule that makes the box usable: "Increased concern for genetic etiology if two or more findings are present."
q_0164.trap: (D) and (E) are the two to reject, and neither appears anywhere in the box. Both sound like plausible pediatric concerns, which is exactly the tactic — a distractor drawn from general pediatrics rather than from the printed list.

q_0165.stem: A nurse tells a mother, "I know exactly how you feel — I was terrified when my own son was admitted." How should this response be classified?
options: Empathy, because the nurse is sharing a comparable experience
Sympathy — having feelings or emotions similar to those of another person, rather than understanding those feelings
A facilitative response
Anticipatory guidance
q_0165.rationale: Sympathy is "having feelings or emotions similar to those of another person, rather than understanding those feelings," while empathy is "the capacity to understand what another person is experiencing from within that person's frame of reference; it is often described as the ability to put oneself in another's shoes" (p. 82).
q_0165.trap: (A) is the reflex pick, and the book defines the two terms against each other on the same page, which is the shape of the item. The discriminator is whose frame of reference is being used: empathy enters the parent's, while sympathy substitutes the nurse's own.

q_0166.stem: A nurse asks a father about his son's eating, then interrupts to finish his sentence, offers reassurance before he has described the problem, and moves on to the next question. Which behaviors from Box 4.2 does this show? (Select all that apply.)
options: Interrupting and finishing the person's sentence
Offering premature or inappropriate reassurance
Deliberately changing the focus
Constant fidgeting or attempting to move away
Frequently looking at a watch or clock
q_0166.rationale: Box 4.2 is two lists, and the split between them is the point: communication barriers are what the nurse does wrong, and signs of information overload are how the patient signals it (p. 82).
q_0166.trap: (D) and (E) are the two to reject, and both are real entries from the same box — they belong to the patient-overload column, not the nurse-barrier one. An option can be a genuine item from the printed box and still be the wrong half of it. Note the correction the chapter names for the nurse side: "One of the best methods for improving interviewing skills is audiotape or videotape feedback."

q_0167.stem: A mother falls silent partway through describing her son's behavior problems. What should the nurse do?
options: Introduce a new topic to relieve the discomfort
Allow the silence, which permits the interviewee to sort out thoughts and feelings and search for responses, and can also be a cue for the interviewer to go more slowly
Fill the pause by summarizing what has been discussed so far
End the interview, since the mother has finished
q_0167.rationale: Silence "permits the interviewee to sort out thoughts and feelings and search for responses to questions. Silence can also be a cue for the interviewer to go more slowly," and "Breaking a silence by introducing a new topic or by prolonged talking essentially terminates the interviewee's opportunity to use the silence" (p. 82).
q_0167.trap: (A) and (C) both fill the pause, which is the instinct the chapter names and rejects. When a silence does need breaking, the chapter's example is a question that keeps the floor with the parent: "Is there anything else you wish to say?"

q_0168.stem: A nurse is interviewing a family through a hospital interpreter. Which actions are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Communicate directly with family members when asking questions, without ignoring the interpreter
Pose questions to elicit only one answer at a time
Refrain from interrupting family members and the interpreter while they are conversing
Arrange for the family to speak with the same interpreter on subsequent visits whenever possible
Ask the interpreter privately what she thinks of the family's understanding while the family is present
q_0168.rationale: The Nursing Care Guidelines direct the nurse to explain the purpose to the interpreter beforehand, introduce the interpreter and allow time for acquaintance, communicate directly with family members, ask one-answer questions ("Do you have pain?" rather than "Do you have any pain, tiredness, or loss of appetite?"), avoid interrupting, avoid medical jargon, and use the same interpreter on later visits (p. 83).
q_0168.trap: (E) is the one to reject, and the chapter gives the reason plainly: "Avoid commenting to the interpreter about family members because they may understand some English."

q_0169.stem: A 12-year-old is fluent in English and offers to interpret for her non-English-speaking mother during a history. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept, since the child is willing and fluent
Decline; the use of children in health care interpreting is strongly discouraged, and use a professional interpreter or a telephonic language line instead
Accept for the history but not for the physical examination
Accept if the mother consents
q_0169.rationale: "the use of children in health care interpreting is strongly discouraged because they are often not mature enough to understand health care questions, answers, or messages." Children "may inadvertently commit interpretive errors, such as inaccuracies, omissions, or substitutions," "can be adversely affected by serious or sensitive information," and in some cultures using a child "is considered an insult to an adult because children are expected to show respect by not questioning their elders." Some institutions prohibit it outright; the alternative named is "a language line using a telephonic interpreter" (p. 83).
q_0169.trap: (D) is the most defensible-sounding wrong answer, and it misplaces the objection. The problem is not consent — it is accuracy, the burden placed on the child, and in some cultures the insult to the adult.

q_0170.stem: A nurse enters an examination room and immediately kneels in front of a shy 3-year-old, smiles broadly, makes eye contact, and asks him about his toy. What is the likely effect?
options: The child will feel welcomed and relax
Anxiety will increase — active attempts to make friends with children before they have had an opportunity to evaluate an unfamiliar person tend to increase their anxiety
The approach is correct because the nurse is at the child's level
The effect depends entirely on the child's temperament
q_0170.rationale: "Active attempts to make friends with children before they have had an opportunity to evaluate an unfamiliar person tend to increase their anxiety," and the guidelines direct the nurse to "Avoid sudden or rapid advances, broad smiles, extended eye contact, or other gestures that may be seen as threatening" (pp. 83–84). The move is to keep talking to the parent while doing something that does not involve the child.
q_0170.trap: (C) names a real guideline — "Assume a position that is at the same level as the child" — and applies it at the wrong moment. Being at eye level is right; arriving there before the child has had time to evaluate you is not. Broad smiles and extended eye contact appear on the chapter's list of potentially threatening gestures, not reassuring ones.

q_0171.stem: A 4-year-old is told she will feel "a little stick in the arm." She becomes distressed and looks for a stick. What accounts for this?
options: She is developmentally delayed
Children in early childhood interpret words literally, and the chapter uses this exact example
She is exhibiting regression from the stress of hospitalization
The explanation was given too far in advance
q_0171.rationale: Children younger than 5 "interpret words literally" and attach literal meaning to phrases such as "two-faced," "sticky fingers," or "coughing your head off"; a child told they will get "a little stick in the arm" may not envision an injection (p. 84). The related instruction under vital signs is to "avoid using the word 'take' when measuring vital signs because young children interpret words literally and may think that their temperature or other function will be taken away."
q_0171.trap: (A) reads normal preoperational thinking as a deficit. The same egocentrism means the chapter says it is "futile to use another child's experience in an attempt to gain the cooperation of small children" — focus communication on the child in front of you.

q_0172.stem: A 9-year-old is scheduled for a procedure and keeps asking why it is being done and how the equipment works. How should the nurse respond?
options: Redirect the questions, since detailed explanations increase anxiety at this age

Give explanations and reasons, since school-age children want them and are interested in the functional aspect of all procedures — and they need to know what is going to take place and why it is being done to them specifically
Answer only through a doll or puppet
Defer all explanations to the parent
q_0172.rationale: School-age children "rely less on what they see and more on what they know," "want explanations and reasons for everything but require no verification beyond that," "are interested in the functional aspect of all procedures," and "need to know what is going to take place and why it is being done to them specifically" (p. 85).
q_0172.trap: (C) is the technique for a *young* child — communicating through transition objects such as dolls, puppets, and stuffed animals before questioning directly — applied several stages too late. Note the school-age child's other feature: "a heightened concern about body integrity" that extends to possessions, so they "may appear to overreact to loss or threatened loss of treasured objects."

q_0173.stem: A 15-year-old who has been managing her own diabetes for years becomes tearful and asks her mother to stay during a painful procedure. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: As regression requiring referral
As normal: adolescents fluctuate between child and adult thinking and behavior, and when tensions rise they may seek the security of the more familiar and comfortable expectations of childhood
As evidence she is not ready to self-manage her condition
As manipulation to avoid the procedure
q_0173.rationale: Adolescents "fluctuate between child and adult thinking and behavior," and "when tensions rise, they may seek the security of the more familiar and comfortable expectations of childhood." The chapter states the balance directly: "It is as much a mistake to regard an adolescent as an adult with an adult's wisdom and control as it is to assume that the teenager has the concerns and expectations of a child" (p. 85).
q_0173.trap: (C) draws a durable conclusion from a momentary shift, which is exactly the error the chapter's two-sided warning is written against. Note also that privacy and confidentiality are "of great importance" at this age "because it is consistent with developmental maturity and autonomy."

q_0174.stem: A nurse is beginning a visit with a 16-year-old and his mother, and time is limited. What should the nurse do?
options: Interview the parent first in every case, since the parent is the informant
Interview the adolescent first in every case

Either order is defensible — talking with the adolescent first immediately identifies with the young person, and talking with the parents first may provide insight into the family relationship — but give both parties an opportunity to be included, and state at the onset that time is limited to avoid appearing to take sides
Interview them together only, so nothing is concealed
q_0174.rationale: Talking with the adolescent first "has the advantage of immediately identifying with the young person"; talking with the parents first "may provide insight into the family relationship." Either way, "give both parties an opportunity to be included," and if time is limited say so at the onset "to avoid appearing to 'take sides'" (p. 85).
q_0174.trap: (D) forecloses the private conversation the chapter treats as essential — older children should be given "the opportunity to talk without parents present," and nurses must know state and federal consent and confidentiality laws for suspected abuse, substance use, suicidal or homicidal ideation, contraceptive care, pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, and sexual assault.

q_0175.stem: A nurse says to an adolescent, "You are being uncooperative about doing your treatments." Which technique should replace this, and why?
options: A third-person statement, because it is less threatening
An I-message: "I am concerned about how the treatments are going because I want to see you get better" — because you-messages are judgmental and provoke defensiveness
A facilitative response
Mutual storytelling
q_0175.rationale: The technique is to "Relate a feeling about a behavior in terms of 'I.'... Avoid use of 'you.' 'You' messages are judgmental and provoke defensiveness," and the chapter gives this exact contrast (p. 85).
q_0175.trap: (A) names a different real technique for a different purpose. The third-person technique expresses a feeling as "he," "she," or "they," which "allows children three choices: (1) to agree and, one hopes, express how they feel; (2) to disagree; or (3) to remain silent" — useful for eliciting, not for correcting a behavior.

q_0176.stem: A hospitalized child says she is scared the other children will laugh at her scar. The nurse replies, "You feel worried because you think the other kids will notice." Which technique is this?
options: Facilitative response
Bibliotherapy
Storytelling
Sentence completion
q_0176.rationale: A facilitative response reflects feelings and content back: "Listen carefully and reflect back to patients the feelings and content of their statements," with the formula "You feel _ because _." Such responses "are empathic and nonjudgmental and legitimize the person's feelings" (p. 85).
q_0176.trap: (C) is the nearest relative and works the other direction. Storytelling uses "the language of children to probe into areas of their thinking while bypassing conscious inhibitions or fears"; mutual storytelling goes further, with the nurse retelling the child's story with therapeutic differences, and the chapter calls it the "more therapeutic approach than storytelling."

q_0177.stem: A nurse is evaluating a child's drawing of her family. Which principles apply? (Select all that apply.)
options: Use spontaneous drawings and evaluate more than one drawing whenever possible
Interpret the drawing as a whole rather than focusing on specific details
Size expresses importance, power, or authority
Exclusion of a family member may denote a feeling of not belonging or a desire to eliminate
A single drawing is sufficient to establish a diagnosis of family dysfunction
q_0177.rationale: The guidelines for evaluating drawings state each of the keyed items, and add that the order drawn "expresses priority in terms of importance," the child's position relative to others "expresses feelings of status or alliance," and erasures, shading, or cross-hatching "expresses ambivalence, concern, or anxiety" (p. 87).
q_0177.trap: (E) is the one to reject and it contradicts the first two principles at once — more than one drawing, and the whole rather than the detail. Drawing is called "one of the most valuable forms of communication — both nonverbal (from looking at the drawing) and verbal (from the child's story of the picture)," and the verbal half is why a single image is not read as a finding.

q_0178.stem: A clinic is short on time and considers replacing the interview with a written questionnaire the parent completes. What does the chapter say?
options: The indirect method is preferred because it is more complete
The direct method is superior; if the indirect route must be used, review the parents' written responses and question them regarding any unusual answers
The two methods are equivalent
The indirect method should be used for all initial visits
q_0178.rationale: The history format may be direct, "in which the nurse asks for information via direct interview with the informant," or indirect, "in which the informant supplies the information by completing some type of questionnaire. The direct method is superior" (p. 88).
q_0178.trap: (A) inverts the chapter's ranking. Note the related Nursing Alert if translated forms are used: "be certain the informant is literate in the foreign language" — a written form assumes a literacy the interview does not.

q_0179.stem: A nurse begins a visit by asking, "How is your son sick?" How should this opening be evaluated?
options: Appropriate, because it is open ended
It is a labeling-type question and should be avoided; elicit the chief complaint with open-ended, neutral questions such as "What seems to be the matter?" or "Why did you come here today?"
Appropriate only for a well-child visit
It is too broad and should be replaced with a closed-ended question
q_0179.rationale: Elicit the chief complaint with "open-ended, neutral questions (e.g., 'What seems to be the matter?,' 'How may I help you?,' or 'Why did you come here today?'). Avoid labeling-type questions (e.g., 'How are you sick?' or 'What is the problem?')" (p. 88). If the parent names many problems, ask which one prompted them to seek help now.
q_0179.trap: (D) moves in the wrong direction. Closed-ended questions are named among the blocks to communication — "limiting expression of emotion by asking directed, closed-ended questions." The fault in the stem's question is the label it plants, not its breadth.

q_0180.stem: A 7-year-old reports abdominal pain. Which approach best establishes the location?
options: Accept the description "stomach pains" and document it
Have the child point with one finger to where it hurts, or point to where a parent would put a bandage — and for radiation, ask the child to show with a finger where the pain goes
Ask the parent to indicate the location on the child's body
Palpate each quadrant and note where the child withdraws
q_0180.rationale: "'Stomach pains' is too general." Have the child "point with one finger to where it hurts" or "point to where mommy or daddy would put a Band-Aid," and for radiation: "Does the pain stay there or move? Show me with your finger where the pain goes" (p. 89). Type, location, severity, duration, and influencing factors are the five components of symptom analysis; for type, "Record whatever words they use in quotes."
q_0180.trap: (A) is the failure the chapter names by name, and it is what makes location a technique rather than a question. Note that severity is "best determined by finding out how it affects the child's usual behavior" — pain that prevents playing, interacting, sleeping, and eating is most often severe.

q_0181.stem: A parent reports that her child walked without assistance at 6 months. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: As evidence of advanced motor development, to be documented as reported
As a clue to misunderstanding of the requested activity, prompting a more specific question
As a reason to refer for developmental evaluation
As unreliable recall that should be omitted from the record
q_0181.rationale: The chapter directs the use of specific questions, because "'sitting up' can mean many different activities," and "A clue to misunderstanding of the requested activity may be an unusually early age of achievement" (p. 90).
q_0181.trap: (A) is the reflex reading of an impressive milestone, and it is exactly backwards — an implausibly early age is more likely to mean the parent and nurse are describing different behaviors than that the child was precocious.

q_0182.stem: A nurse is taking a sexual history from a 16-year-old. Which approach does the chapter recommend?
options: Ask whether the adolescent is "sexually active," since it is the standard clinical term
Ask "Are you having sex with anyone?" — probably the most direct and best understood question — and refer to all sexual contacts in nongender terms, such as "partners"
Ask the parent to leave and then ask about girlfriends or boyfriends by name
Defer sexual history to the provider
q_0182.rationale: "avoid asking whether the adolescent is 'sexually active' because this term is broadly defined. 'Are you having sex with anyone?' is probably the most direct and best understood question." Because same-sex experimentation may occur, "refer to all sexual contacts in nongender terms, such as 'partners,' rather than 'girlfriends' or 'boyfriends'" (pp. 90–91).
q_0182.trap: (A) is the clinical habit the chapter singles out as too vague to yield an answer. (C) gets the privacy half right and then reintroduces the gendered assumption. Compare the chemical-use phrasing on the same pages, which works the same way: "Many kids your age are experimenting with drugs and alcohol; have you ever had any drugs or alcohol?" yields more reliable data than "How much do you drink?"

q_0183.stem: A nurse examines a quiet 4-month-old in the parent's lap. Which sequence is correct?
options: Proceed strictly head to toe, beginning with the eyes and ears

Auscultate heart, lungs, and abdomen while the infant is quiet; then palpate and percuss the same areas; then proceed head to toe, performing traumatic procedures last and eliciting the Moro reflex last of all
Elicit all reflexes first while the infant is calm, then examine body systems
Begin with the most painful area so it is not anticipated
q_0183.rationale: Table 4.2 gives the infant sequence: "If quiet, auscultate heart, lungs, abdomen. Record heart and respiratory rates. Palpate and percuss same areas. Proceed in usual head-to-toe direction. Perform traumatic procedures last (eyes, ears, mouth [while crying]). Elicit reflexes as body part is examined. Elicit Moro reflex last" (p. 98).
q_0183.trap: (A) confuses the recording order with the examination order. The head-to-toe order is kept for *recording*; the examination itself is reordered by age to minimize stress, preserve the parent-child relationship, and "Maximize the accuracy and reliability of assessment findings." (D) reverses the standing rule that painful areas are examined last — except in an emergency, where airway, breathing, circulation, and the injured area come first.

q_0184.stem: A nurse wants to introduce the stethoscope to a 2-year-old before auscultating. What does Table 4.2 direct?
options: Demonstrate the equipment's use on a parent, then on the child
Allow the toddler to inspect the equipment; demonstrating its use is usually ineffective
Explain the purpose of the equipment and its significance
Explain the findings as they are obtained
q_0184.rationale: The toddler column states: "Allow toddler to inspect equipment; demonstrating use of equipment is usually ineffective" (p. 98).
q_0184.trap: (A) and (C) are both correct — for older children. The Preparation column runs a developmental ladder: the toddler is *shown nothing* because demonstration does not work, the preschooler gets a *brief* demonstration, the school-age child gets the *purpose* explained ("otoscope to see eardrum, which is necessary for hearing"), and the adolescent gets the *findings* explained during the examination. Choosing the rung is the item.

q_0185.stem: A nurse is deciding whether a preschooler is ready to cooperate with the examination. Which are the chapter's signs of readiness? (Select all that apply.)
options: Talking to the nurse
Making eye contact
Accepting the offered equipment
Choosing to sit on the examining table rather than the parent's lap
Remaining silent and still when approached
q_0185.rationale: The signs are "Talking to the nurse; Making eye contact; Accepting the offered equipment; Allowing physical touching; Choosing to sit on examining table rather than parent's lap" (p. 98).
q_0185.trap: (E) is the one to reject and it reads compliance as consent. Silence and stillness are not on the list; when the readiness signs are absent, the chapter's move is to talk to the parent while "essentially 'ignoring' child," make complimentary remarks, tell a funny story or a simple magic trick, or use a hand puppet as a nonthreatening friend.

q_0186.stem: Three siblings are to be examined at one visit, and one is visibly anxious. What does the chapter direct?
options: Examine the anxious child first to get it over with
Begin with the most cooperative child to model desired behavior
Examine all three simultaneously to save time
Reschedule the anxious child for a separate visit
q_0186.rationale: "If several children in the family will be examined, begin with the most cooperative child to model desired behavior" (p. 98).
q_0186.trap: (A) is a defensible-sounding instinct that forfeits the modeling opportunity the chapter is pointing at — and the anxious child watching a sibling go first is the intervention.

q_0187.stem: A 5-year-old refuses to be examined and begins to cry. Which actions does the chapter direct?
options: Give a prolonged, detailed explanation of the procedure until the child agrees

Assess the reason for the refusal, involve child and parent, avoid prolonged explanations, use a firm direct approach, perform the examination as quickly as possible, have an attendant gently restrain, and limit the number of people in the room
Postpone the examination indefinitely
Remove the parent from the room to reduce the child's audience
q_0187.rationale: These are the chapter's directions when a child refuses, and it notes that "a child who is unduly afraid may have had a traumatic experience" (p. 98).
q_0187.trap: (A) is the intuitive escalation and is specifically ruled out — "Avoid prolonged explanations about examining procedure." (D) inverts one of the five reasons the sequence is altered in the first place: to "Preserve the essential security of the parent-child relationship, especially with young children."

q_0188.stem: A nurse is plotting growth for an 18-month-old and a 4-year-old. Which charts should be used?
options: CDC charts for both
WHO growth standards for the 18-month-old and CDC growth charts for the 4-year-old
WHO standards for both
CDC charts for the 18-month-old and WHO standards for the 4-year-old
q_0188.rationale: The WHO growth standards are used "to monitor growth for infants and children between the ages of 0 and 2 years old," because they "reflect growth patterns among children who were predominately breastfed," and "The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention growth charts... are used for children 2 years old and older" (pp. 98–100).
q_0188.trap: (D) swaps the two age bands, which is the only way this pair is tested. The rationale for the split is worth holding: the WHO standard is a breastfed reference, which is why it belongs to the years when breastfeeding is most common.

q_0189.stem: A nurse needs to measure a 14-month-old. What is the correct method?
options: Standing height on a stadiometer, since the child can walk
Recumbent length on a length board, holding the head in midline, grasping the knees together gently, and pushing down until the legs are fully extended
A tape measure laid alongside the infant on the examining table
Either method, as long as it is documented
q_0189.rationale: Measure recumbent length until 24 months (or 36 months if using the birth-to-36-months chart) using a length board, extending the body by "(1) holding the head in midline, (2) grasping the knees together gently, and (3) pushing down on the knees until the legs are fully extended" (p. 100).
q_0189.trap: (C) is wrong twice over — wrong instrument and wrong position — and the chapter rules the instrument out explicitly: "A tape measure should not be used to measure the length of infants and children because the methods are inaccurate and unreliable." Note the related alert for older children: "Normally height is less if measured in the afternoon than in the morning," so serial measurements are taken at the same time of day.

q_0190.stem: A 9-year-old's BMI-for-age plots at the 87th percentile. How is this classified?
options: Healthy weight
Overweight
Obese
Underweight
q_0190.rationale: The BMI-for-age and gender categories are "underweight (<5th percentile), healthy weight (5th to <85th percentile), overweight (≥85th percentile and <95th percentile), or obese (≥95th percentile)" (p. 104).
q_0190.trap: (C) is the classic error the fact bank names — a distractor placing obesity at the 85th percentile. The 85th opens the overweight band; obesity begins at the 95th. This is the same cut point Chapter 1 uses, so getting it wrong costs twice.

q_0191.stem: Which growth patterns does the chapter identify as questionable and warranting further investigation? (Select all that apply.)
options: Height and weight percentiles that are widely disparate
Failure to follow the expected growth velocity in height and weight
A sudden increase or decrease in a previously steady pattern — crossing two major percentile lines after 3 years old
Short stature in the absence of short parents
Consistent tracking along the 10th percentile for both height and weight
q_0191.rationale: These are the four patterns the chapter lists (p. 100). The interpretive principle behind them: "the most reliable evaluation lies in comparing growth measurements over time because they reflect change," and "same-age children (whether short, average, or tall in stature) should grow at similar rates."
q_0191.trap: (E) is the one to reject, and it is chosen by anyone who reads a low percentile as a problem. A child tracking steadily along any percentile is following an expected velocity — it is the *crossing* that matters, and only after 3 years old.

q_0192.stem: A nurse measures head circumference on a 15-month-old and finds it equal to the chest circumference. How should this be interpreted, and through what age is head circumference routinely measured?
options: Abnormal; head circumference should always exceed chest circumference in childhood
Expected — head and chest circumferences are equal at about 1 to 2 years of age — and head circumference is measured routinely up to 36 months and in any child whose head size is questionable
Abnormal; chest should already exceed head by 5 to 7 cm at this age
Expected, and head circumference is measured routinely only through 12 months
q_0192.rationale: "Generally, head and chest circumferences are equal at about 1 to 2 years of age. During childhood, chest circumference exceeds head size by about 5 to 7 cm (2 to 2.75 inches)." Head circumference is measured "in children up to 36 months of age and in any child whose head size is questionable," at "its greatest frontooccipital circumference" (p. 104).
q_0192.trap: (C) applies the later childhood relationship at the crossover age. Note the technique detail: use paper or nonstretchable tape "because a cloth tape can stretch and give a falsely small measurement."

q_0193.stem: A nurse must obtain vital signs on a sleeping 5-month-old. In what order should they be taken?
options: Temperature, pulse, respirations
Respirations first (before the infant is disturbed), pulse next, temperature last
Pulse, respirations, temperature
Any order, provided all three are obtained
q_0193.rationale: For infants, "count respirations first (before the infant is disturbed), take the pulse next, and measure temperature last" (p. 105). If the vital signs cannot be taken without disturbing the child, "record the child's behavior (e.g., crying) along with the measurement."
q_0193.trap: (A) is the adult habit and it reverses the ordering principle — least disturbing to most. Note that in infants respirations are counted by observing abdominal movements, "because respirations are primarily diaphragmatic," and for a full minute "Because the movements are irregular."

q_0194.stem: A 3-week-old needs an accurate temperature. Which route is recommended, and why?
options: Rectal, since it is the clinical gold standard
Axillary, because rectal temperature is contraindicated for infants younger than 1 month old due to risk of rectal perforation, and axillary is the recommended screening route at this age
Oral, since it is the standard for noninvasive measurement
Tympanic, since it is fastest
q_0194.rationale: Rectal "remains the clinical gold standard" but is "contraindicated for infants younger than 1 month old due to risk of rectal perforation," and the chapter's bottom line states: "For infants younger than 1 month of age, axillary temperatures are recommended for screening" (pp. 105–106).
q_0194.trap: (A) is true as a general statement and unsafe in this patient, which is the shape of every route question in this chapter. (C) fails on a different age gate: oral is contraindicated under 5 years of age, as well as in children with altered level of consciousness, receiving oxygen, mouth breathing, or with mucositis or recent oral surgery.

q_0195.stem: An axillary temperature on a 2-year-old reads 37.2° C (99° F). A nurse suggests adding a degree to estimate the core temperature. How should this be evaluated?
options: Correct; adding 1° F to an axillary reading approximates core temperature
Incorrect; the belief that core temperature can be estimated by adding a degree to an axillary temperature is named and rejected — do not add a degree
Correct, but only for children older than 1 year
Incorrect; a degree should be subtracted instead
q_0195.rationale: The Nursing Alert states: "The belief that core temperature can be estimated by adding 1° F to the temperature taken in the axilla is incorrect. Do not add a degree to the finding obtained by taking a temperature by the axillary route" (p. 106).
q_0195.trap: (A) is a widely taught rule of thumb the chapter names specifically in order to reject it. Note also the limitation on the route itself: axillary "is inconsistent and insensitive in infants and children over 1 month old" and is usable "as a screening tool for fever in young, clinically stable infants and children."

q_0196.stem: A nurse is assessing pulses on a 10-month-old. Which approach is correct?
options: Radial pulse, counted for 30 seconds and doubled
Apical pulse, counted for 1 full minute, because in infants and young children the apical impulse is more reliable and irregularities in rhythm are possible
Radial pulse, counted for 1 full minute
Carotid pulse, counted for 15 seconds
q_0196.rationale: "A satisfactory pulse can be taken radially in children older than 2 years of age. However, in infants and young children, the apical impulse... is more reliable," and "Count the pulse for 1 full minute in infants and young children because of possible irregularities in rhythm" (p. 106).
q_0196.trap: (A) fails on both counts — wrong site for the age and a shortcut interval that assumes a regular rhythm. Note the separate screening rule from this section: "Compare radial and femoral pulses at least once during infancy to detect the presence of circulatory impairment, such as coarctation of the aorta."

q_0197.stem: A child's pedal pulse is easy to palpate and is not easily obliterated with pressure. How is this graded?
q_0197.rationale: Table 4.4 grades pulses 0 to +4, and +3 is "Easy to palpate, not easily obliterated with pressure (normal)" (p. 107).
q_0197.trap: (D) is the reflex pick for a learner who assumes a strong pulse is the top of the scale. It is not: +4 is "Strong, bounding, not obliterated with pressure," which is abnormal. The normal grade sits one step below the maximum, which is what makes this scale worth memorizing rather than reasoning through.

q_0198.stem: A nurse selects a blood pressure cuff for a child. What determines the correct size?
options: The label on the cuff, such as "infant" or "child"
A bladder width approximately 40% of the arm circumference midway between the olecranon and the acromion, which usually gives a bladder length covering 80% to 100% of the arm circumference
A bladder width covering 80% to 100% of the arm circumference
The width of the child's hand
q_0198.rationale: "the most important factor in accurately measuring BP is the use of an appropriately sized cuff (cuff size refers only to the inner inflatable bladder, not the cloth covering)." Choose "a cuff with a bladder width that is approximately 40% of the arm circumference midway between the olecranon and the acromion," which usually gives "a cuff bladder length that covers 80% to 100% of the circumference of the arm" (p. 108).
q_0198.trap: (C) swaps the two percentages between width and length. (A) is ruled out by name: "Do not choose a cuff based on the name of the cuff (e.g., an 'infant' cuff may be too small for some infants)."

q_0199.stem: The correctly sized cuff is unavailable and the nurse must choose between one that is too small and one that is too large. Which should be used, and what error will result?
options: The undersized cuff, which will read falsely low
The oversized cuff, accepting a falsely low reading — the chapter directs using an oversized cuff rather than an undersized one
The undersized cuff, accepting a falsely high reading
Neither; defer the measurement
q_0199.rationale: "If the cuff size is too small, the reading on the device is falsely high. If the cuff size is too large, the reading is falsely low," and the Nursing Alert directs: "When the correct size is not available, use an oversized cuff rather than an undersized one" (p. 108).
q_0199.trap: (A) is the mirror error and the fact bank calls this the single most swapped pair in the chapter. Note why the direction of the preference makes sense clinically: an oversized cuff underestimates, so it will not manufacture a false diagnosis of hypertension — but it can mask a real one, which is why size selection is called the most important factor.

q_0200.stem: An automated oscillometric device reads a child's blood pressure above the 90th percentile. What is the next step?
options: Document the reading and refer for hypertension evaluation
Repeat the elevated reading using auscultation, since oscillometric readings are generally about 10 mm Hg higher and the two methods are not interchangeable
Repeat with the same device on the opposite arm
Recheck the reading in one week
q_0200.rationale: Oscillometric readings "are generally higher (10 mm Hg higher) than measurements using auscultation," and the two "prevent the interchange of the readings by the two methods." The directive is explicit: "An elevated BP reading obtained with an oscillometric device should be repeated using auscultation" (p. 108). Auscultation "remains the recommended method."
q_0200.trap: (A) acts on a number the chapter says is systematically high. The related Nursing Alert underlines it: "Published norms for blood pressure are valid only if you use the same method of measurement (auscultation and cuff size determination) in clinical practice."

q_0201.stem: A 16-year-old's blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, which falls below the 90th percentile for his age, sex, and height. How should this be classified?
options: Normotensive, since it is below the 90th percentile
Prehypertensive — if an adolescent's blood pressure is more than 120/80 mm Hg, consider the patient prehypertensive even if the value is below the 90th percentile
Stage 1 hypertension
Stage 2 hypertension
q_0201.rationale: A child is normotensive "if the BP is below the 90th percentile"; the 90th to 95th percentile is prehypertension; at or above the 95th is possible hypertension, requiring repeat "on at least two occasions to confirm diagnosis." And: "if an adolescent's BP is more than 120/80 mm Hg, consider the patient prehypertensive, even if this value is below the 90th percentile" (p. 109).
q_0201.trap: (A) applies the percentile rule correctly and misses the adolescent override, which is the whole point of the item. Blood pressure is measured annually in children 3 years of age through adolescence, so this is a routine finding rather than an unusual one.

q_0202.stem: A teenager reports fainting when he stands up quickly. The nurse measures blood pressure supine and again after 2 minutes standing, finding a 24 mm Hg systolic drop with a heart rate increase of 8 beats/min. How should this be interpreted?
options: A normal postural response
Orthostatic hypotension most likely due to an autonomic deficit, because the sustained systolic drop exceeds 20 mm Hg without an increase in heart rate of more than 15 beats/min
Orthostatic hypotension from a nonneurogenic cause such as hypovolemia
The measurement is invalid because 2 minutes is too short
q_0202.rationale: "The child with a sustained drop in systolic pressure of more than 20 mm Hg or in diastolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg after standing for 2 minutes without an increase in heart rate of more than 15 beats/min most likely has an autonomic deficit. Nonneurogenic causes of OH have a compensatory increase in pulse of more than 15 beats/min, as well as a drop in BP" (p. 109). Measurement is taken "at least 2 minutes in each position."
q_0202.trap: (C) is the mirror reading of the same numbers and the more common cause overall — hypovolemia, "which may be induced by medications such as diuretics, vasodilator medications, and prolonged immobility or bed rest." What separates the two is the pulse response, not the pressure drop: a compensatory rise above 15 beats/min points away from an autonomic deficit.

q_0203.stem: A 4-year-old's corneal light reflex is symmetric, but her epicanthal folds give the appearance that one eye turns inward. How should this be documented?
options: Strabismus, requiring referral
Pseudostrabismus — the false impression of misalignment created by epicanthal folds, with symmetric corneal light reflexes
Amblyopia
Normal binocularity, no further testing indicated
q_0203.rationale: Epicanthal folds are "excess folds of skin that extend from the roof of the nose to the inner termination of the eyebrow and that partially or completely overlap the inner canthus of the eye," and may give the "false impression of misalignment" called pseudostrabismus. In the corneal light reflex test, symmetric light in each pupil is orthophoric — normal (p. 114).
q_0203.trap: (A) diagnoses from appearance alone, which is the distractor the fact bank flags for this pair. The test result, not the look of the eyes, is what settles it. (C) names the consequence rather than the finding: strabismus is the misalignment, and amblyopia is the "blindness from disuse" that follows "if it is not detected and corrected by 4 to 6 years old."

q_0204.stem: A 7-year-old tests 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. Both results are within the passing range for his age. What should the nurse do?
options: Record as normal, since both eyes pass
Refer — a two-line difference between the eyes is referable on its own, even within the passing range
Repeat the test at the next well visit
Refer only if the child reports symptoms
q_0204.rationale: Table 4.6 lists as a referral criterion at 6 years and older: "Two-line difference between eyes, even within the passing range (i.e., 10/10 and 10/15 or 20/20 and 20/30)" (p. 115).
q_0204.trap: (A) is the reflex pick and is exactly the trap the fact bank names: a child reading 20/20 in one eye and 20/30 in the other has two passing eyes and still gets referred. The interocular difference is a separate criterion from the acuity threshold, not a softer version of it.

q_0205.stem: A nurse examines a 6-month-old and finds a white pupillary reflex on one side. What does this indicate?
options: A normal variant in infants
A possible retinoblastoma, requiring referral; a brilliant, uniform red reflex is what rules out many serious defects of the cornea, aqueous chamber, lens, and vitreous chamber
Cataract only
Pseudostrabismus
q_0205.rationale: The Nursing Alert states: "A brilliant, uniform red reflex is an important sign because it rules out many serious defects of the cornea, aqueous chamber, lens, and vitreous chamber. Any dark shadows or opacities are recorded because they indicate some abnormality," and a white reflex "indicates possible retinoblastoma" (p. 114). Ocular media clarity referral criteria in Table 4.6 are "White pupil, dark spots, absent reflex."
q_0205.trap: (C) names one real cause of an abnormal reflex and stops short of the finding that makes this urgent. The red reflex is a screen for several conditions at once, which is why the chapter describes what a *normal* one rules out rather than listing what an abnormal one means.

q_0206.stem: A nurse is performing pure tone audiometry screening on a school-age child. Which frequencies and threshold define a failure?
options: 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz, failing if the child cannot hear the tones at 20 dB
250, 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz, failing at 40 dB
1000, 2000, 4000, and 8000 Hz, failing at 20 dB
500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz, failing at 40 dB
q_0206.rationale: The AAP "recommends pure tone audiometry testing screening at 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz, with children failing if they cannot hear the tones at 20 dB" (p. 119). Universal newborn hearing screening is available in all US states, and the quality indicator is children 3 months of age or younger who received an audiological evaluation.
q_0206.trap: (D) keeps the right frequencies and doubles the threshold, which would let a mild loss pass. The chapter's Research Focus explains why the threshold is set low: "failure to identify children even with mild high-frequency hearing loss may have long-term consequences."

q_0207.stem: A nurse auscultating a child's heart notes that the split in S2 does not change during inspiration. What does this suggest?
options: Physiologic splitting, a significant normal finding
Fixed splitting, an important diagnostic sign of atrial septal defect
An S3 gallop
A normal finding in all school-age children
q_0207.rationale: The Nursing Alert states: "Fixed splitting, in which the split in S2 does not change during inspiration, is an important diagnostic sign of atrial septal defect." Normally "the split of the two sounds in S2 is distinguishable and widens during inspiration. Physiologic splitting is a significant normal finding" (p. 125).
q_0207.trap: (A) is the mirror error and the pair turns on one word: physiologic splitting widens on inspiration, fixed splitting does not change. The discriminator is the respiratory variation, not the presence of a split.

q_0208.stem: A nurse hears a third heart sound in a healthy 8-year-old. How should this be interpreted, and what would change the interpretation?
options: S3 always indicates heart failure and requires referral
S3 is normally heard in some children; S4 is rarely heard as a normal heart sound and usually indicates the need for further cardiac evaluation
Both S3 and S4 are normal findings in children
Neither S3 nor S4 is ever audible in a healthy child
q_0208.rationale: S3 "is normally heard in some children. S4 is rarely heard as a normal heart sound; it usually indicates the need for further cardiac evaluation" (p. 125). The chapter's mnemonics: S3 "sounds like word S1 S2 S3: 'Ken-tuc-ky'"; S4 "sounds like word S4 S1 S2: 'Ten-nes-see.'"
q_0208.trap: (A) imports the adult significance of an S3. Note the technique that goes with these sounds: use "both diaphragm and bell chest pieces when auscultating heart sounds. Bell chest piece is necessary for low-pitched sounds of murmurs, S3, and S4."

q_0209.stem: A nurse auscultates over a child's manubrium and upper intrascapular region and hears inspiration that is louder and higher pitched than the sounds heard elsewhere over the lung fields. How should this be classified?
options: Vesicular breath sounds, which are abnormal in this location
Bronchovesicular breath sounds, which are expected over the manubrium and upper intrascapular regions where the trachea and bronchi bifurcate
Adventitious sounds requiring further evaluation
Bronchial sounds, which are normal over the entire lung surface
q_0209.rationale: Bronchovesicular breath sounds are "Heard over the manubrium and in the upper intrascapular regions where trachea and bronchi bifurcate. Inspiration is louder and higher pitched than in vesicular breathing." Vesicular sounds are "Heard over entire surface of the lungs, with exception of upper intrascapular area and area beneath the manubrium," where "Inspiration is louder, longer, and higher pitched than expiration. The sound is a soft, swishing noise" (p. 122).
q_0209.trap: (A) has the right sound type and the wrong location logic — vesicular sounds are normal everywhere *except* the two regions named in the stem, so the exception in one definition is the rule in the other. Chapter 26 relies on this terminology, so the classification is worth holding precisely.

q_0210.topic: pain physiology and consequences of untreated pain
q_0210.stem: A nurse hesitates to medicate a postoperative child, reasoning that pain is unpleasant but not harmful. How should this be corrected?
options: The reasoning is sound if the pain is short lived

Pain triggers physiologic stress responses with negative consequences involving multiple systems; long-term amplification of the sympathetic nervous system hinders healing, and unrelieved pain may prolong the stress response and adversely affect recovery
The concern applies only to neonates
Pain becomes harmful only once it becomes chronic
q_0210.rationale: "Pain triggers a number of physiologic stress responses in the body, and these may lead to negative consequences involving multiple systems. Long-term amplification of the sympathetic nervous system hinders healing. Unrelieved pain, whether from trauma, surgery, or disease, may prolong stress response and adversely affect a child's recovery" (pp. 137–138).
q_0210.trap: (D) reverses the direction of the relationship the chapter draws. Poorly controlled acute pain "predisposes patients to chronic pain syndromes" — acute pain left untreated is one of the ways chronic pain begins, not a separate and lesser problem.

q_0211.topic: pain physiology and consequences of untreated pain
q_0211.stem: A preterm infant who has had many heel sticks now cries and becomes rigid during routine repositioning and diaper changes. What explains this?
options: The infant has become manipulative and is seeking attention

The wind-up phenomenon — after noxious stimuli, multiple levels of the spinal cord experience altered excitability, which may cause normal nonpainful stimuli such as routine nursing care and handling to be perceived as noxious
Normal irritability of prematurity, unrelated to prior procedures
An adverse effect of analgesia
q_0211.rationale: The wind-up phenomenon is "attributed to a decreased pain threshold and chronic pain"; after noxious stimuli "multiple levels of the spinal cord experience an altered excitability," which "may cause normal nonpainful stimuli, such as routine nursing care and handling, to be perceived as noxious stimuli" (p. 138). Neonates "have more generalized spinal reflex responses and lower thresholds to stimuli than older children."
q_0211.trap: (C) treats an acquired, mechanistic change as constitutional temperament, and it removes the reason to act. Wind-up is why repeated procedural pain in a preterm infant is a compounding problem rather than a series of isolated events.

q_0212.topic: pain physiology and consequences of untreated pain
q_0212.stem: A nurse describes bandage removal, nasogastric tube placement, and urinary catheter placement as routine rather than painful. How should this be evaluated?
options: Accurate; these are noninvasive and are not associated with pain
Inaccurate; the chapter names each of these explicitly as very painful to children, and warns that nurses may find it easy to overlook such experiences as part of normal care
Accurate for children over 5 years old
Inaccurate only for the nasogastric tube
q_0212.rationale: "Nurses may find it easy to overlook certain painful experiences as part of normal care and perform invasive procedures without any attempts to minimize pain. Something as minor and ordinary as bandage removal, nasogastric tube placement, or urinary catheter placement is very painful to children" (p. 138). Premature infants "are particularly vulnerable to repeated acute pain episodes from routine and frequent procedures."
q_0212.trap: (A) is the working assumption the chapter is written to dislodge — the risk is not disbelieving a child's pain report but never asking, because the procedure was not categorized as painful in the first place.

q_0213.topic: pain physiology and consequences of untreated pain
q_0213.stem: A child reports pain at a site where no tissue injury can be identified, and a nurse suggests the pain is not real. How should this be addressed?
options: The nurse is correct; pain requires an identifiable physical source

Once pain tracks are created in the brain, it is possible for pain to exist purely in the brain — and that pain is real, and it feels the way the child says it feels, regardless of the location of origin
The child should be evaluated for a psychiatric disorder before pain is treated
The report should be documented but not treated
q_0213.rationale: "Once these pain tracks are created in the brain, it is possible for pain to exist purely in the brain. This pain, however, is real and it feels the way the child says it feels — regardless of the location of origin" (p. 138). The brain neuromatrix is "a series of connected neural cells with cognitive, sensory, and affective pathways combined in a feedback loop unique to each individual."
q_0213.trap: (C) makes treatment conditional on ruling out a psychological cause, which reverses the chapter's stance. The origin of the pain does not determine whether it is real or whether it is treated.

q_0214.stem: A verbal 9-year-old rates his pain 8 out of 10 while lying quietly and watching television. His FLACC score is 1. Which assessment should guide management?
options: The FLACC score, because behavioral observation is more objective than self-report
The child's self-report, because self-report is the single most reliable indicator of pain and must be accepted and respected as the most important pain assessment data available
An average of the two scores
Neither; repeat both in an hour
q_0214.rationale: "Self-report is the single most reliable indicator of pain and must be accepted and respected by nurses as the most important pain assessment data available" (p. 145). Observational measures are the fallback for children who cannot self-report, and "Pain scores on observational measures do not correlate with children's own reports of pain intensity" (p. 144).
q_0214.trap: (A) is the central inversion of this chapter and it is the reason quiet children go untreated. An observational tool measures behavioral and physiologic responses, not perceived intensity — the two are different constructs, so a low behavioral score does not overrule a high self-report. (C) treats two incommensurable measures as averageable.

q_0215.stem: A nurse is deciding whether to use an observational pain measure for a 10-year-old with chronic abdominal pain. What does the chapter say about the tool's validity here?
options: Observational measures are equally valid at all ages and for all pain types

Observational measures are most reliable for short, sharp procedural pain such as heel lance or injection; they are less reliable for acute pain and are not reliable or valid for chronic pain or for pain in older children
Observational measures are preferred for chronic pain because they avoid reporting bias
Observational measures are valid for chronic pain but not procedural pain
q_0215.rationale: "Observational pain measures are most reliable when used to measure short, sharp procedural pain, such as pain due to heel lance or injections. They are less reliable when measuring acute pain and not reliable or valid for assessing chronic pain or pain in older children" (p. 144).
q_0215.trap: (C) is the convenience answer for a busy unit and it fails on two counts at once — wrong pain type and wrong age. The related reason acute tools fail in chronic pain: "Tools that measure acute pain intensity may not be sensitive to the subtle changes and slow resolution characteristic of chronic and recurrent pain because pain expression becomes more complex."

q_0216.stem: A child rated 5 on one unit and 5 on another, and a nurse concludes the pain is unchanged. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw; a 5 is a 5

Scores are not interchangeable — a pain score of 5 may mean a lot of pain on a 0 to 5 scale or very little on a 0 to 100 scale — and consistent use of the same measurement tool is necessary to standardize communication and evaluate effectiveness
The second score should have been doubled
Pain scores should never be compared across time
q_0216.rationale: "A pain score of 5 may mean a lot of pain (if a 0 to 5 scale is used) or very little (if a 0 to 100 scale is used)," and "Consistent use of the same measurement tools is necessary to standardize communication related to pain and evaluate the effectiveness of pain management strategies" (p. 143).
q_0216.trap: (D) overcorrects into abandoning serial comparison entirely, which is the whole purpose of consistent tool use. Comparison across time is the point; comparison across *tools* is what fails, and the deeper reason is that different tools measure different pain expressions.

q_0217.stem: A nurse records only a numeric pain rating at each assessment. What else does the chapter require?
options: Nothing further; intensity is the standard measure

Location, frequency, duration, and precipitating, aggravating, and alleviating factors, plus pain's effect on sleep, emotional function, physical recovery or functioning, disability, role functioning, and satisfaction with pain treatment
Only the analgesic given and the time
Vital signs, which substitute for the additional dimensions
q_0217.rationale: "Pain assessment should be more thorough than merely obtaining a pain rating. Understanding the location, frequency, duration, and precipitating, aggravating, and alleviating factors of the pain experienced by the child is also essential," along with pain's effect on the domains listed (p. 143). Other dimensions "may change without a change in pain intensity."
q_0217.trap: (D) substitutes physiologic signs for the assessment, which is a version of the same error as trusting a behavioral score over a self-report — vital signs are a response to pain, not a measure of its dimensions.

q_0218.stem: A nurse is assessing pain in a nonverbal 6-month-old. Which finding is the most consistent and specific indicator?
options: Heart rate elevation
Facial expression, evaluated through features such as eye squeeze, brow bulge, open mouth, and taut tongue
Oxygen saturation
Duration of crying
q_0218.rationale: "Facial expression is the most consistent and specific indicator of pain in infants," evaluated through features such as "eye squeeze, brow bulge, open mouth, and taut tongue" (p. 143).
q_0218.trap: (A) and (C) are physiologic parameters that appear inside several scales as scored variables, which makes them plausible — but neither is singled out as the most consistent and specific indicator, and both change for many reasons other than pain.

q_0219.stem: A 4-year-old is recovering in the postanesthesia care unit and is too drowsy to self-report. Which tool is validated for this situation?
options: COMFORT-B
FLACC
Wong-Baker FACES
CRIES
q_0219.rationale: "The only tool found reliable and valid for pain assessment of children 2 months to 7 years of age recovering in the postanesthesia care unit is the FLACC tool" (p. 145). FLACC scores five behaviors — Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability — each 0 to 2, for a total of 0 to 10.
q_0219.trap: (A) is the right idea in the wrong setting, and it is the item's whole point. COMFORT-B belongs to the critically ill, ventilated, nonverbal child; FLACC is the one with PACU validation. This pair sorts by setting, not by the child's alertness.

q_0220.stem: A 6-year-old is mechanically ventilated and sedated in the PICU. Which tool is most appropriate, and what score suggests pain?
options: FLACC, with pain considered above 5
COMFORT-B, with pain considered above 17 on a 6 to 30 scale
Numeric Rating Scale, with pain considered above 4
NIPS, with pain considered above 4
q_0220.rationale: The COMFORT-B is "one of the most commonly used pain scales to assess critically ill ventilated children who are nonverbal due to sedation or their condition" and "is particularly helpful in children who are mechanically ventilated." Its range is 6–30, and the table's note reads "Consider pain >17" (pp. 144–145). It scores alertness, calmness/agitation, respiratory response or crying, physical movement, muscle tone, and facial tension.
q_0220.trap: (A) attaches the FLACC score range to the right kind of child but the wrong tool, and (D) uses an infant scale on a school-age child. Both score ranges and age ranges have to travel with the tool name.

q_0221.stem: A nurse must choose an infant pain scale for a neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation who is being assessed after surgery. Which scale's age range excludes this infant?
options: PIPP-revised, 25–40 weeks
N-PASS, 23–40 weeks
CRIES, 32–40 weeks
NIPS, 26–40 weeks
q_0221.rationale: Table 5.4's age ranges are in gestational weeks: PIPP-revised 25–40, NIPS 26–40, N-PASS 23–40, COMFORT-neo 24–42, and CRIES 32–40 (p. 144). At 28 weeks this infant falls below the CRIES range.
q_0221.trap: CRIES is otherwise the intuitive pick, because it is the postoperative scale and the stem supplies a postoperative context — which is exactly why the age column has to be read alongside the type-of-pain column. (A) is the reflex rejection, since PIPP-revised sounds like the specialized tool with the narrowest window; its range comfortably includes 28 weeks.

q_0222.stem: Which infant pain scales adjust the score for gestational age?
options: NIPS and CRIES
PIPP-revised and N-PASS
COMFORT-neo and CRIES
All five adjust for gestational age
q_0222.rationale: Of the five scales in Table 5.4, only PIPP-revised and N-PASS carry a gestational-age adjustment (p. 144). PIPP-revised scores heart rate, oxygen saturation, brow bulge, eye squeeze, nasolabial furrow, and behavioral state 0–3 each, for a range of 0–21; N-PASS scores vital signs, crying/irritability, facial expressions, behavioral state, and extremities/tone 0–2 each, for a pain range of 0–10.
q_0222.trap: (D) is the reasonable assumption that any scale designed for neonates must account for maturity, and it is wrong for three of the five. Note that CRIES scores Crying, requiring Oxygen, Increased vital signs, Expression, and Sleeplessness — its acronym is the mnemonic, and it is a postoperative tool for the 32-to-40-week infant.

q_0223.stem: A 3-year-old needs a self-report pain scale. Which is validated at this age, and what is the caution?
options: Faces Pain Scale–Revised, which starts at a neutral face

Wong-Baker FACES, validated for children as young as 3 years — but smiling faces on pain assessment scales may lead younger children to rate the affective domain of pain rather than its intensity, so simple concrete anchor words should be used
Numeric Rating Scale, since 3-year-olds can count
Visual Analog Scale, since it is nonverbal
q_0223.rationale: Wong-Baker FACES uses "six cartoon faces ranging from smiling face for 'no pain' to tearful face for 'worst pain'" and is "For children as young as 3 years old." The caution: "smiling faces on pain assessment scales may lead younger children to rate the affective domain of pain; or, in other words, rate their feelings about having pain rather than report the intensity of their physical pain," mitigated by using "Simple, concrete anchor words, such as the script originally used to validate the tool" (pp. 145–146).
q_0223.trap: (A) is the right instinct about the smiling-face problem applied to the wrong age — the Faces Pain Scale–Revised starts at a neutral face precisely because of that concern, but it is validated for children 5 to 17, not for a 3-year-old.

q_0224.stem: A 6-year-old needs a faces scale, and the nurse wants to avoid the affect problem. Which scale starts with a neutral rather than a smiling face, and what is its age range?
options: Wong-Baker FACES, 3 years and up
Faces Pain Scale–Revised, for children 5 to 17
Oucher, 3 to 13 years
Word-Graphic Rating Scale, 8 to 17 years
q_0224.rationale: The Faces Pain Scale–Revised uses "six cartoon faces ranging from neutral face for 'no pain' to grimacing face 'worst possible pain'" and is for children 5–17 (p. 146).
q_0224.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, and the starting face is the entire discriminator between these two scales — smiling for Wong-Baker, neutral for the revised scale. Both have six faces and both are cartoons, so nothing else separates them at a glance.

q_0225.stem: A nurse plans to use the Oucher photographic scale with a 5-year-old. What must the child be able to do first?
options: Count off any two numbers or count by 10s
Rate six geometric shapes from largest to smallest
Read the descriptive words on the scale
Nothing; the photographic scale requires no prerequisite
q_0225.rationale: The Oucher provides "six photographs of a white child's face representing 'no hurt' to 'biggest hurt you could ever have;' also includes vertical scale with numbers from 0-100; scales for African American and Hispanic children have been developed," for children 3–13. For the photographic scale the child "should be able to rate six geometric shapes from largest to smallest" (p. 146).
q_0225.trap: (A) is the prerequisite for the Oucher's numeric scale, not its photographic one — the same tool has two halves with two different readiness tests. Note also the chapter's finding on the ethnic versions: an "Ethnically similar scale may not be preferred by child when given choice of ethnically neutral cartoon scale."

q_0226.stem: An 8-year-old is being asked to rate pain. Which scale is most widely used in clinical practice, and which do children least prefer?
options: The Visual Analog Scale is most widely used; children least prefer the Numeric Rating Scale
The Numeric Rating Scale is most widely used because it is easy to use; research shows children ages 3 to 18 least prefer the Visual Analog Scale
Both are equally used and equally preferred
The Word-Graphic Rating Scale is most widely used
q_0226.rationale: "The numeric rating scales (NRSs), such as the 0 to 10 scale, are the most widely used in clinical practice because they are easy to use," and of the VAS: "Research shows that children ages 3-18 years old least prefer VAS compared with other scales" (pp. 146–147). Both are used from about 8 years.
q_0226.trap: (A) swaps the two, which is the only way this pair is tested. Both scales share an age floor of about 8 years, so the discriminator is preference and practicality, not developmental readiness.

q_0227.stem: At what age do the cognitive skills required for a numeric rating scale appear, and can a younger child report pain at all?
options: Seriation appears between 7 and 10 years, so most school-age children can use a numeric scale — and even 2-year-olds can report pain
Numeric scales can be used from 3 years, and children under 3 cannot report pain
Seriation appears at 5 years, and children under 5 cannot report pain
Numeric scales require 12 years of age
q_0227.rationale: The cognitive skills of "measurement, classification, and seriation (the ability to accurately place items in rank order), become apparent between 7 and 10 years of age. Therefore most school-age children have the cognitive ability required to use a numeric rating scale." Self-report measures "are most often used for children older than 3 to 4 years, but even 2-year-olds can report pain" (p. 145).
q_0227.trap: (B) and (C) both convert a scale's readiness threshold into a claim that younger children cannot report pain. Those are different statements: the age boundary governs which *tool* fits, not whether the child has something to tell you. "Although children at 3 or 4 years of age are able to self-report pain, they do not have the cognitive ability to understand rank order," which is why faces scales exist.

q_0228.stem: A preterm infant lies still and shows no facial grimace during a heel stick. What should the nurse conclude?
options: The infant is not experiencing pain

Preterm infants' responses to pain may be behaviorally blunted or absent, so it is imperative to presume that pain exists in all situations usually considered painful for adults and children, even in the absence of behavioral or physiologic signs
The observational score should be recorded as zero and no analgesia given
The infant has a high pain threshold
q_0228.rationale: "Preterm infants' responses to pain may be behaviorally blunted or absent," and the rule that follows is that "it is imperative to presume that pain exists in all situations that are usually considered painful for adults and children, even in the absence of behavioral or physiologic signs" (pp. 144–145).
q_0228.trap: (D) inverts the physiology. Neonates have "lower thresholds to stimuli than older children," not higher — the absence of a visible response reflects an immature or overwhelmed capacity to *show* pain, not an absence of feeling it.

q_0229.stem: A neonate is receiving vecuronium. How should pain be assessed and managed?
options: Behavioral observation scales remain valid because muscle tone is scored

An infant receiving a muscle-paralyzing agent is incapable of a behavioral or visible pain response, yet there is ample evidence such infants are neurologically capable of feeling pain — so pain is presumed and treated
Paralysis eliminates pain perception, so analgesia is unnecessary
Pain should be assessed by heart rate alone
q_0229.rationale: "an infant receiving a muscle-paralyzing agent (vecuronium) is incapable of a behavioral or visible pain response; however, there is ample evidence that such infants are neurologically capable of feeling pain" (p. 145).
q_0229.trap: (C) is the dangerous version of the same misreading, and it is why the chapter states this case separately from the blunted-response one. A paralytic removes the signal, not the sensation. (A) fails because every behavioral variable, muscle tone included, depends on the movement the drug has abolished.

q_0230.stem: A nonverbal 8-year-old with severe cognitive impairment is being assessed for postoperative pain. Which tools are validated, and what does the chapter require when using the revised FLACC?
options: FLACC, COMFORT-neo, and CRIES; no customization is needed

Revised FLACC, the Non-communicating Children's Pain Checklist–Revised, and the Paediatric Pain Profile — and when using the revised FLACC, nurses must include parent-reported pain behaviors to customize the tool to the individual child
Only the Numeric Rating Scale, with parental proxy reporting
Wong-Baker FACES, with the parent selecting the face
q_0230.rationale: The three validated tools are rFLACC, NCCPC-r, and PPP, and "When using the rFLACC, nurses must include parent-reported pain behaviors to customize the tool to use with individual children" (p. 145). Children with cognitive impairment "may not be able to express pain through behaviors or self-report methods validated for developmentally similar peers," and parents report their pain "was not effectively managed."
q_0230.trap: (A) offers a plain FLACC without the revised descriptors, and the difference is not cosmetic — the customization step is what makes the tool valid for this child, because the behaviors that signal pain differ from child to child.

q_0231.stem: A parent of a child with cerebral palsy reports that physical therapy, assisted stretching, and putting on splints are painful. How should the nurse treat this information?
options: As parental over-reporting, since these are therapeutic rather than noxious activities

As accurate and expected: parents of children with cognitive impairment report that ordinary daily activities including assisted stretching and walking, independent standing, toileting, putting on splints, occupational therapy, range of motion, and physical therapy are painful
As a reason to discontinue therapy
As relevant only if the child also cries
q_0231.rationale: Parents reported that these ordinary daily activities were painful, and the most frequent parent-reported pain behaviors include "crying; being less active; seeking comfort; moaning; not cooperating; being irritable; being stiff, spastic, tense, or rigid; sleeping less; being difficult to satisfy or pacify; flinching or moving body part away; and being agitated or fidgety" (p. 145).
